posts.title: Tue 8 Sep, 10:00 — Back boiler out, combi in
posts.caption:
Back boiler out, combi in.

If your heating still runs off a back boiler sat behind the fireplace, this is what it looks like at the other end.

It isn't a like-for-like swap. A back boiler heats a cylinder; a combi heats water on demand — so the cylinder goes, the loft tanks go, and you get mains pressure at every tap.

What people underestimate is everything around it: a new flue, the gas supply checked and upsized to carry the load, the fireplace opening made good, and the whole system flushed before the new boiler ever fires. Skip the flush and you push twenty years of sludge straight into a brand new heat exchanger. That black cylinder at the bottom is the filter that catches whatever's left.

Removing a back boiler is gas work. It needs a Gas Safe registered engineer, not a general builder.

The bit most people mention afterwards isn't the heating — it's getting the airing cupboard back.

Still got a back boiler? Tell us what's putting you off — the disruption, the cost, or just not knowing what's involved. 👇

posts.title: Where the boiler goes changes the job
posts.caption:
This boiler lives in a low cupboard, with the flue taken out through the wall behind it.

Where a boiler goes is one of the biggest things separating two quotes for what looks like the same job.

🚪 Access. Everything that gets touched at a service — the casing, the condensate trap, the expansion vessel — has to be reachable in the space it sits in. Fit it tight and every visit for the next fifteen years takes longer.

📏 The flue route. Length, bends and where it terminates are rules, not preferences. Moving a boiler two feet can change the whole flue job.

🎛️ Controls, while the wall is open. The programmer, the room thermostat and the radiator valves are what decide the running cost. They are cheap to do properly on fitting day and awkward to add afterwards.

🔌 Getting gas and power to it. Not free, and easy to leave off a quote.

None of that shows in a photo of a tidy white box on a wall. All of it is either in the price or missing from it.

If you are getting quotes, ask what changes because of where yours is going: https://cmghp.co.uk/boilers/new-boiler-installation/

Where's yours — kitchen cupboard, loft, garage, under the stairs? 👇

posts.title: Check me before you let me in
posts.caption:
You are letting a stranger into your house to work on gas. You are entitled to know exactly who that is before he arrives — and you should not have to take his word for any of it.

So here is everything, with where to check it:

🔥 Gas Safe registered, 917962. Check it free at https://www.gassaferegister.co.uk — you need nothing but the number.

🔧 CIPHE, 129130. Members are vetted before joining, have to keep their skills current, and answer to an independent complaints panel. Verify at https://www.ciphe.org.uk

💧 WaterSafe approved for work on drinking water. Search BL2 2TA at https://www.watersafe.org.uk

🛡️ £5 million public liability, and 24 months on my own workmanship.

🪪 Every Gas Safe engineer carries an ID card. Look at the expiry date, and look at the back — it lists what that engineer is assessed to work on, and boilers, fires, cookers and commercial work are separate categories.

🚩 Nobody legitimate minds being asked. If somebody bristles at it, that tells you something on its own.

posts.title: The bit of a service you never see
posts.caption:
That cloudy liquid is what your boiler makes while it heats the house. Roughly a couple of litres a day in winter, mildly acidic, and it has to get away somewhere.

This is a condensate trap, off during a service. It is one of the parts that separates a service from a look-over.

💧 It is meant to hold water. That seal is what stops flue gases coming back up the pipe.

🧼 It silts up. Debris settles in it, and a blocked trap locks a boiler out with a fault code that looks far more dramatic than the cause.

❄️ It freezes. A condensate pipe run outside in the wrong size, or with too little fall, is the most common no-heat call of a cold snap — and that is a fitting decision, not bad luck.

🔍 It gets cleaned and put back properly, seal correct. Not glanced at through a gap in the casing.

If a service never involves the case coming off, none of this has been looked at.

What a proper one includes: https://cmghp.co.uk

posts.title: When a flush is worth it, and when it isn't
posts.caption:
Back in August I posted a filter magnet caked in black sludge. The fair question that followed was: right, so does everyone need a power flush then?

No. And it's worth being straight about it, because it is one of the easiest things in this trade to oversell.

Three honest categories:

1️⃣ **Worth it.** Radiators cold at the bottom across the whole house, the system slow to warm, a boiler cutting out on temperature, or black water when you bleed. That is circulation being choked by iron oxide, and cleaning it out is the fix.

2️⃣ **Not worth it on its own.** One cold radiator, a room that never gets warm, or a valve that has stuck. That is usually balancing or a valve, and a flush would be an expensive way to not fix it.

3️⃣ **Worth it as part of something else.** Fitting a new boiler onto an old system. The debris that lived happily in the old boiler will not live happily in the new one's heat exchanger — which is why a system flush and a magnetic filter are included as standard on every install I do rather than sold as an extra.

The bit that saves you the money either way: once a system is clean, a filter keeps it clean, and it takes two minutes to empty at a service.

🛑 Where to stop and call someone: if you are losing pressure, seeing a fault code, or you can smell gas. Gas you can smell is 0800 111 999 first, everything else after.

What do your radiators do — warm at the top, cold at the bottom, or fine? 👇

posts.title: The bits of the job you will never see
posts.caption:
When people compare quotes, they compare the bits they can see. The boiler brand, the tiles, the finish. Fair enough — it's what's in front of you.

But the difference between a job that lasts and a job that gets ripped out in six years is nearly all behind the wall, and it is decided in the first two days.

Four things nobody ever photographs:

🪵 What the fixings go into. A grab rail, a radiator, a wall-hung basin — they either go into timber put in while the wall was open, or into plasterboard and optimism. You cannot tell which by looking, and you will find out eventually.

📐 The fall on the waste and the condensate. Water moves because of a gradient, and the gradient is set before anything is boarded over. Get it wrong and you get smells, gurgling, or a pipe that freezes.

🔧 Whether anything can be got at again. Isolating valves in reachable places, a filter you can open, an inspection point where one is needed. A service in three years is either simple or awkward, and that is decided on fitting day.

🧯 Pipe support and protection. Clipped properly, sleeved where it goes through, not resting its weight on the joints.

None of it costs much extra while the wall is open. All of it costs a fortune later.

So when you're comparing quotes, ask what happens behind the plaster. The answer tells you more than the appliance does: https://cmghp.co.uk

posts.title: "Any plumber can work on a gas boiler"
posts.caption:
MYTH: "A plumber's a plumber. If he can do a bathroom he can sort the boiler."

It's an easy assumption and it is the wrong way round. Plumbing and gas are two different trades that often live in the same van.

🚿 Plumbing is water. Bathrooms, cylinders, leaks, drainage, mains. No register, no card, and plenty of very good people doing it.

🔥 Gas is legally restricted. Working on a gas appliance without being Gas Safe registered is a criminal offence, not a technicality — and registration is by category. Boilers, cookers, fires, water heaters and commercial work are assessed separately and reassessed every five years.

Which is why a genuinely competent engineer can still be the wrong person for the specific job in front of him. It isn't an insult to say so.

What that means for you, practically:

🪪 For anything gas — ask for the card and look at the back for the category, or check the register yourself in thirty seconds at https://www.gassaferegister.co.uk

💧 For anything on drinking water, the equivalent is WaterSafe: https://www.watersafe.org.uk

And the honest bit: I hold both, plus CIPHE membership, which is why I say it out loud rather than hoping nobody asks. My own numbers and where to check them are here: https://cmghp.co.uk/credentials/

🛑 If you can smell gas, none of the above — 0800 111 999, straight away.

Did you know gas registration was split by category? Most people don't 👇

posts.title: Week 3 — w3_co_six_signs
posts.caption:
Carbon monoxide does a cruel thing: it makes you feel like you're coming down with something.

Headache. Dizzy. Out of breath on the stairs. Bit sick. Every one of those gets blamed on a bug, a bad night's sleep, or getting older.

The six signs are headaches, dizziness, breathlessness, nausea, collapse, and loss of consciousness.

But the one that actually gives it away isn't on that list. It's the pattern: you feel rough at home, you feel better when you're out, and it comes back when you walk through the door. If more than one person in the house has it at the same time, or the dog's off too, take that seriously.

You cannot see it, smell it or taste it. An alarm is the only thing that will tell you.

If that pattern sounds familiar — get everyone out, open the doors, and ring 0800 111 999. Free, 24 hours.

This is Gas Safety Week, run by Gas Safe Register: https://www.gassaferegister.co.uk/

Has anyone reading this had a CO alarm go off? What happened? 👇

posts.title: Week 3 — w3_co_alarm_where
posts.caption:
Most houses I go into have a CO alarm. A fair few have it in the wrong place, and a good number have one that stopped working years ago without anybody noticing.

Where it goes matters as much as having one.

One in every room with a gas appliance — not just the boiler. The gas fire and the cooker count.

One to three metres from the appliance, measured across the room, and high up. Carbon monoxide travels with warm air, so near the ceiling is right and skirting-board height is not.

Not in a cupboard. Not behind a curtain. Not directly above the boiler.

Then the bit everyone forgets: press the test button once a month, and check the date on the back. Most have a sealed 7 or 10 year life and then they're done, whatever the light says.

And they are not smoke alarms. Different alarm, different job, and one will not do the other's.

Go and press yours now — takes ten seconds. Did it sound? 👇

posts.title: Week 3 — w3_appliance_warning_signs
posts.caption:
You can't smell carbon monoxide. But an appliance that's producing it usually looks wrong, and you can learn what wrong looks like in about a minute.

🔥 Flames. Gas should burn crisp and blue. Lazy, floppy, yellow or orange flames mean it isn't burning properly.

⚫ Black marks or sooty staining on or around the appliance, or on the wall above a gas fire.

💧 A lot more condensation in the room than you'd expect.

🕯️ A pilot light that keeps going out on its own.

Any of those: stop using the appliance and get a Gas Safe registered engineer to look at it. Don't wait for the service that's due in four months.

Smell gas — 0800 111 999, free, 24 hours.

It's Gas Safety Week and this year's line is "take no chances", which is about right. None of the above is a maybe.

Go and look at your gas fire or hob tonight. Blue, or yellow? 👇

posts.title: Week 3 — w3_vents_airbricks
posts.caption:
Every autumn, somebody seals up an airbrick to stop a draught. It's the most understandable mistake in the house and one of the more dangerous ones.

Gas appliances need air to burn properly. Vents and airbricks are how they get it. Block the air, the appliance can't burn cleanly, and incomplete combustion is where carbon monoxide comes from.

Inside, it's cushions, furniture pushed against a vent, or a bit of card taped over it.

Outside is the one people miss completely. Shrubs grown over an airbrick. A new fence panel right against the wall. Render taken across it. Decking built up over it. None of that feels like blocking a vent, and all of it does.

If there's a vent in your house and you don't know what it's there for — that's the one to ask about before the heating goes on properly.

Draughty house? Fair enough. But get the vents identified first, then draught-proof around them.

Anyone found one blocked up by a previous owner? 👇

posts.title: Week 3 — w3_smell_gas
posts.caption:
If you smell gas, there's an order to do things in, and most people get one step wrong.

1. Open the doors and windows.
2. Turn the gas off at the meter — the handle beside it, quarter turn so it sits across the pipe.
3. Don't touch any switches. Not on, not off. A switch makes a tiny spark either way, so leave the light, the extractor and the alarm panel alone.
4. No naked flames, and don't smoke.
5. Get outside and ring 0800 111 999.

That's the National Gas Emergency number. It's free, it's answered 24 hours, and you will not be charged for them coming out. They will make it safe.

The step people get wrong is number three — reaching for a light switch on the way out of a dark room is pure instinct.

Worth reading this once now rather than trying to remember it later.

Screenshot it, or stick 0800 111 999 in your phone. Have you got it saved? 👇

posts.title: Week 3 — w3_landlord_cp12
posts.caption:
If you rent a property out, this one's a legal duty rather than good practice.

Every gas appliance and flue checked every 12 months by a Gas Safe registered engineer. You get a gas safety record — the CP12.

The tenant gets a copy within 28 days of the check. A new tenant gets it before they move in. You keep the records for two years.

The part landlords underestimate: without a valid CP12 you may find your insurer won't play, and you can't serve a Section 21. For one visit a year, it's the cheapest piece of paper you'll ever buy.

One flat, one HMO or a handful of terraces — the duty is identical.

And if you've inherited a property and can't find any record of a check ever being done, that's the one to sort first, not last.

Landlords: how do you keep track of when each one is due? 👇

posts.title: W4/5 — w4_outside_tap
posts.caption:
The outside tap is the first thing in the house to freeze, and the damage never shows up outside.

Water sat in a short run of pipe with cold air either side of it. It freezes, it expands, and the split usually happens in the bit of pipe inside the wall. You find out in the thaw when the kitchen ceiling goes.

Three minutes to sort:

Find the isolator — normally a small valve on the pipe just inside the wall the tap comes through, often under the sink or in a cupboard. Turn it off. Then go outside, open the tap, and let what's left drain out.

Leave the tap open all winter. Water that can't drain is water that can freeze.

No isolator anywhere? Lag the pipe and put an insulated cover over the tap — and get an isolator fitted before next winter, because you'll want one eventually anyway.

Worth doing now rather than the night they forecast minus four.

posts.title: W4/5 — w4_balancing
posts.caption:
One radiator you can't touch, another in the back bedroom that never gets past lukewarm. That's not a broken radiator — it's balance.

Water is lazy. It takes the shortest, easiest route back to the boiler, which is usually the radiators nearest it. The ones at the far end get whatever's left.

Balancing is throttling the easy ones so the water is forced round the hard ones. It's done at the lockshield valve — the plain one with the little cap, not the one with numbers on. Each radiator gets set so the temperature drop across it is about right, in order, with a thermometer.

Two things worth knowing before you assume that's your problem:

Cold at the top and warm at the bottom is air, not balance — that one's a bleed key and five minutes.

And if a radiator is cold at the bottom instead, that's something else again and worth having looked at.

Balancing is a proper job done once and then left alone for years.

Which room in your house is always the cold one? 👇

posts.title: W4/5 — w4_test_run
posts.caption:
Turn your heating on this week. Not because you need it — because you don't.

Twenty minutes is enough. Then walk round the house and actually put your hand on every radiator, top and bottom, including the spare room nobody goes in from March to November.

Listen to it. Banging, gurgling or whistling is the system telling you something. Far better it tells you in September.

Check the programmer fires when it says it will, and that the hot water still comes on separately if it's supposed to.

Here's the honest reason. A fault found now is a normal appointment at a normal time. The same fault on the first properly cold morning is you in a queue behind everyone else who did the same thing, in the week every heating engineer in Bolton is flat out.

Nothing else in the house gets left six months and then expected to work perfectly first go.

Go and put it on. What did yours sound like? 👇

posts.title: W4/5 — w4_where_pipes_freeze
posts.caption:
Loft insulation does exactly what it says — it keeps the heat in the house. Which means everything above it is now sat in an unheated space.

That catches people out every year. The loft used to get a bit of warmth leaking up through the ceiling. Insulate properly and it doesn't any more, so pipes that were fine for twenty years are suddenly exposed.

What wants doing:

Lag the pipes in the loft, and lay the insulation UNDER them, never over the top. Insulation on top cuts them off from what little warmth is left.

The cold water tank gets a jacket on the sides and the lid — and the floor underneath it left clear, for the same reason.

Then the ones everyone forgets: pipe runs through a garage, a cellar, an outbuilding, or boxed into an unheated porch.

A burst in a loft empties itself into the ceilings before anybody hears a thing. Lagging is the cheapest insurance in the house.

Been in your loft lately? 👇

posts.title: W4/5 — w4_radiator_blockers
posts.caption:
Before you decide a radiator is broken, check it's allowed to work.

Four things that stop a perfectly good radiator heating a room:

A sofa in front of it. The heat goes into the back of the sofa and stays there. Move it six inches out and you'll feel the difference.

Long curtains hanging over it. All the warm air gets funnelled straight up the cold window and out. Tuck them behind, or get them shortened.

A shelf or a radiator cover. Radiators work by convection — warm air rising off them and circulating. Box one in and you've stopped the mechanism.

Paint. Layer after layer of gloss really does slow the heat coming off it. One or two coats is nothing. Eight coats over forty years isn't.

None of that costs anything to test. Move one thing this week and see whether the cold room warms up.

If it's still cold after that, then it's worth a look.

Which one are you guilty of? 👇

posts.title: W4/5 — w4_hidden_leak
posts.caption:
You can find a hidden leak yourself in about an hour, with nothing but your water meter and a bit of patience.

Turn every tap off. Make sure nothing is filling — no washing machine, no dishwasher, no toilet quietly running. That last one catches people out constantly.

Read the meter and write it down. All of it, including the red dial or the last digits, because a slow leak won't move the big numbers.

Leave it an hour. Touch nothing.

Read it again. Any movement at all means water is going somewhere it shouldn't.

That test tells you whether you've got a leak. It doesn't tell you where — and that's the important bit, because water travels. It runs along joists and under floors and comes out a long way from the split.

So if it has moved, don't start lifting floorboards where the damp patch is. That's rarely where the leak is.

Tracing it properly is a separate job with proper kit.

posts.title: W4/5 — w4_check_on_someone
posts.caption:
A favour to ask, and it takes two minutes.

If you've got a parent, a neighbour or anyone older on your street, ask them straight out whether their heating works.

Not "are you alright" — they'll say yes. Ask whether the house is warm and whether the hot water's working. Those are questions with real answers.

A lot of people won't ring anybody about heating until it's been off for days. Sometimes it's not wanting to be a bother. Sometimes it's worrying what it'll cost. Either way they sit in a cold house and say nothing.

Have a look at the radiators yourself if you can. Cold ones get explained away — "oh that one's always been like that".

And while you're stood there, check they've got a carbon monoxide alarm and press the button on it.

Cold homes make people genuinely ill, and it stacks up quietly over a winter rather than happening all at once.

Two minutes in September is worth a great deal in January.

Who are you going to ask? 👇

posts.title: W4/5 — w4_hot_water_cold
posts.caption:
Heating's fine. Hot water's stone cold. It sounds like a strange combination and it's actually one of the more common calls.

On a combi, that pattern usually points at the diverter valve — the part inside that decides whether the heat goes to the radiators or the taps. If it sticks on heating, that's exactly what you get.

With a hot water cylinder it's more likely the cylinder thermostat, a motorised valve, or the immersion if you're running on that.

Before you ring anyone, check the boring stuff: is the hot water actually programmed on, and has anyone had a fiddle with the timer? It happens more than you'd think, especially in a house with teenagers.

One thing that genuinely helps when you do ring — say whether it's stone cold or just lukewarm. They're different faults and it changes what gets brought to the job.

All of this is inside the appliance or the controls, so it's Gas Safe work, not a have-a-go.

posts.title: W4/5 — w5_clock_change
posts.caption:
25 October, the clocks go back. Your phone sorts itself out. Your heating programmer very possibly won't.

If it doesn't, the heating comes on an hour late every single morning right through winter, and most people never work out why the house feels cold when they get up. They just turn the thermostat up and pay for it.

Older dial programmers have a small clock knob on the front you turn round. Digital ones have a set-time button, usually under the flap. Five minutes either way.

While you're stood there, worth checking the on and off times still match when the house is actually lived in. A lot of programmers are still set for a household that moved out, or a work pattern that changed two jobs ago.

Put a reminder in your phone for the 25th now, while you're thinking about it.

It is comfortably the most common "my heating's gone funny" of the whole year, and it isn't a fault at all.

posts.title: W4/5 — w5_banging_pipes
posts.caption:
That bang in the pipes when someone turns a tap off quickly — it's called water hammer, and it isn't just a noise.

Water moving through a pipe has momentum. Shut a valve suddenly and all that momentum has to go somewhere, so it slams into the pipework as a shock wave. That's the bang.

The usual culprits are a quick-closing tap, or the solenoid valve in a washing machine or dishwasher, which shuts almost instantly by design.

What turns it from a click into a bang through the whole house is pipework that isn't clipped properly. Loose pipe under a floor has room to move, and it does.

It's fixable — better clipping, a proper arrestor, and sometimes just easing the incoming pressure at the stop tap.

Worth doing rather than living with. That repeated shock works away at joints and fittings for years. It's a noise now and a leak later.

Does yours bang? Which appliance sets it off? 👇

posts.title: W4/5 — w5_drain_down
posts.caption:
Why does the same job take an hour at one house and half a day at another? Usually this.

Most plumbing jobs can be isolated — valves either side of whatever's being changed, water off to that one thing, everything else in the house carries on as normal.

But if there are no isolation valves, or there are and they've seized solid, the only way to work is to drain the system down. That's a different job entirely: draining, doing the work, refilling, bleeding everything, re-pressurising, checking for leaks.

Same tap. Completely different afternoon.

Which is why it's worth asking, whenever you're having anything done: can isolation valves go in while this is already apart? They're a small part and almost no extra labour at that moment, and they make every future job on that fitting quicker and cheaper.

It's the single best bit of future-proofing in a house and almost nobody asks for it.

If you're having work done this autumn, ask the question 👇

posts.title: W4/5 — w5_shower_temperature
posts.caption:
Someone runs the kitchen tap and your shower goes cold. Or worse, scalding.

On a combi that's two outlets competing for one heat exchanger. The flow to the shower drops, the boiler is still putting the same heat in, and the temperature swings.

A thermostatic shower valve is specifically designed to stop that happening — it senses the change and adjusts to hold the temperature. So if yours is swinging, either there isn't one, or the one you've got has stopped working.

They do stop working. The cartridge inside sticks or furs up. That's a replaceable part, not a new shower and not a new bathroom, whatever anyone tells you.

Going scalding rather than cold is the one to take seriously. In a house with young children, or anyone elderly or unsteady on their feet, an unreliable shower valve isn't an annoyance — it's a scald risk.

Cold is irritating. Hot is dangerous.

Does yours do this? Cold or hot? 👇

posts.title: W4/5 — w5_loft_tank
posts.caption:
Water trickling down the outside wall of the house, usually from a little pipe sticking out high up. That's an overflow, and something inside has failed to stop filling.

Nine times out of ten it's a ball valve — in a loft tank or in a toilet cistern. The float should rise and shut the water off. When it doesn't, the water keeps coming and the overflow pipe does its job, which is to take it outside rather than through your ceiling.

So the overflow running isn't the fault. It's the safety device working.

It's not dramatic, but it doesn't fix itself and it wastes water continuously — day and night, for however long you leave it.

The reason to sort it before winter rather than after: in a hard freeze that overflow pipe can ice up. Then the water has nowhere to go and it backs up into the loft instead.

If you can see one running, get it booked now while it's still just a nuisance.

Seen one on your house? 👇

posts.title: Weekend — w4b_myth_bleeding
posts.caption:
Sunday myth, and it's one nearly everybody believes.

"You should bleed your radiators every autumn."

You bleed a radiator when it's cold at the top and warm at the bottom. That's air sat in the top of it, and the key lets it out. That's the whole rule. It isn't a calendar job like testing a smoke alarm.

Here's the bit worth knowing. A sealed heating system shouldn't be making air. If you're bleeding the same radiator twice a year, something is drawing air in — and that's worth finding rather than living with.

Could be a small leak somewhere pulling air back as the system cools. Could be the pressure dropping and being topped up over and over. Could be a corroding component quietly producing gas inside the system.

So: bleeding is a two-minute job and perfectly normal. Bleeding the same one, over and over, is a symptom.

Anyone got a radiator they bleed every few months? That one's worth mentioning 👇

posts.title: Weekend — w4b_before_frost
posts.caption:
Three jobs worth half an hour of your Saturday, before the first proper frost.

Drain the outside tap. Find the isolator inside — usually a small valve on the pipe just inside the wall — turn it off, then open the tap outside and let it drain. Leave it open all winter. Water that can't drain is water that can freeze, and the split usually happens inside the wall where you won't see it until the thaw.

Lag the pipes in the loft. And lay the insulation UNDER them, not over the top. Insulation on top cuts a pipe off from the last bit of warmth coming up through the ceiling, which is exactly how a well-insulated loft ends up with frozen pipes.

Run the heating for twenty minutes. Feel every radiator top and bottom. Listen for anything new. A fault found in October is a normal appointment. The same fault in the first cold snap is a queue.

None of that needs a tradesman and all of it saves one.

Which one are you doing first? 👇

posts.title: Weekend — w5b_myth_smart_stat
posts.caption:
Sunday myth: "there's no point getting a smart thermostat, my boiler's too old."

Most smart controls replace the room thermostat, not the boiler. If your heating has a thermostat on the wall now, there's a good chance a smart one will go in its place and work fine — whether the boiler is two years old or fifteen.

What actually differs is how it talks to the boiler. Some need a wire running back. Some use a small wireless receiver wired in near the boiler. Occasionally an older setup makes it awkward, but "too old" on its own is rarely the answer.

The honest caveat: a smart stat saves money by heating the house only when somebody's in it. If your heating is already set sensibly and someone's home all day, the saving is smaller than the adverts suggest. It's a control upgrade, not a magic one.

Worth asking what yours would need before you buy anything, because the answer decides whether it's a simple swap or a bit of wiring.

Anyone fitted one? Did it actually change your bills? 👇

posts.title: BWD — bwd_condensation_or_leak
posts.caption:
Condensation, damp or a leak? Three different problems, and they all look like a wet wall.

Condensation turns up on cold surfaces — windows, outside walls, behind a wardrobe pushed flat against the wall. It's worst first thing in the morning and it improves when a room is aired.

Rising or penetrating damp stays low on the wall, or tracks in from outside where there's a problem with a gutter, a gully or the pointing. It doesn't come and go with how well aired the room is.

A leak is a patch that keeps growing and never really dries, regardless of ventilation.

Getting the cause right first matters more than the fix. Wiping condensation off what's actually a leak, or opening windows at a burst pipe, wastes a whole winter and the wall gets worse the whole time.

Which one do you think yours is?

Published by CMG Heating & Plumbing, Bolton · Gas Safe 917962

posts.title: BWD — bwd_boiler_switch
posts.caption:
A question worth asking yourself tonight: do you know which switch turns your boiler off?

Nearly every boiler is fed from a fused spur — a small switched plate, usually beside the boiler or in the airing cupboard. That switch is how you stop it if it starts leaking, banging, or doing anything it shouldn't.

Plenty are hidden. Behind a cupboard door, under boxing-in, occasionally in a completely different room from a previous layout.

Worth finding now rather than when you're standing in water. Label it if it isn't obvious, and tell everyone in the house where it is.

It's the difference between an emergency and an inconvenience.

Do you know where yours is? Go and have a look.

Published by CMG Heating & Plumbing, Bolton · Gas Safe 917962

posts.title: BWD — bwd_burst_pipe
posts.caption:
If a pipe bursts, there's an order to do things in and the order matters.

Water off at the stopcock. Then open the cold taps to drain what's still sat in the pipes, so it goes down the sink rather than through the ceiling.

Electrics next. If water is anywhere near a light fitting, a socket or the consumer unit, switch off at the fuse board.

Heating off if it's a heating pipe, so the boiler isn't firing into a system that's emptying itself.

Then ring somebody. Not before — those three take about a minute between them and they're the difference between a wet floor and a new ceiling.

And the thing to do today rather than then: go and check your stopcock actually turns. A tap you can't shut off in a hurry isn't much of a stopcock, and they seize shut over the years.

Found yours? Does it turn?

Published by CMG Heating & Plumbing, Bolton · Gas Safe 917962

posts.title: BWD — bwd_mould_corner
posts.caption:
It's almost never a coincidence which corner the mould picks.

Mould grows where the wall is coldest, because that's where warm moist air hits a cold surface and condenses. Which is why it turns up in external corners, behind furniture pushed flat against an outside wall, and around window reveals — every one of those is a cold spot.

So wiping it off treats the symptom. The corner is still the coldest bit of the room next week.

What actually changes it is ventilation, a gap behind the furniture so air can move, and enough warmth reaching that surface to keep it above the point where moisture condenses.

If it comes back in the same place every winter, that spot is telling you something about the wall — sometimes insulation, sometimes a cold bridge, occasionally something wrong outside.

Does yours always appear in the same place?

Published by CMG Heating & Plumbing, Bolton · Gas Safe 917962

posts.title: BWD — bwd_draughts
posts.caption:
Not every hole in the wall is a mistake, and this is the time of year people start sealing things up.

Block freely: the letterbox, the keyhole, gaps under doors, rattling sash windows, an unused chimney with a proper cap that still lets a little air through.

Never block: an airbrick, a wall vent, or a grille anywhere near a gas appliance. Those are there to feed combustion air, and they were put there on purpose.

Outside counts as much as inside. Shrubs grown over an airbrick, a new fence panel tight to the wall, render taken across one, decking built up over them — nobody decides to block a vent, it just happens.

Starve a gas appliance of air and it can't burn cleanly. Incomplete combustion is where carbon monoxide comes from.

If there's a vent in your house and you don't know why it's there, find out before you cover it up.

Anyone found one blocked by a previous owner?

Published by CMG Heating & Plumbing, Bolton · Gas Safe 917962

posts.title: BWD — bwd_price_cap
posts.caption:
Your energy bill changes tomorrow, and two things move at once in opposite directions.

The Ofgem price cap rises 4% from 1 October to 31 December. A typical dual-fuel household paying by direct debit goes from £1,663 to £1,723 a year — about £5 a month if that level held for a full year.

But at the same time, VAT on domestic electricity drops from 5% to zero until 31 March. Gas keeps its 5%.

So the increase isn't spread evenly. Gas costs are rising around 8%. Electricity barely moves, and households that use little or no gas will see a much smaller change.

The bit that catches people out every quarter: the cap limits the unit rates and the standing charge, not your total bill. If you use more, you pay more, cap or no cap.

If you're on a standard variable tariff and on the cap, get a meter reading in before tomorrow so the old rates stop where they should.

Source: Ofgem, 26 August 2026.

Published by CMG Heating & Plumbing, Bolton · Gas Safe 917962

posts.title: BWD — bwd_water_off
posts.caption:
Water gone off? Four things to check before you ring anybody.

Is it one tap or the whole house? One tap with the rest fine is usually a problem at that tap rather than a supply issue.

Check your stopcock. They get knocked, especially the ones under the kitchen sink surrounded by cleaning bottles, and a partly closed one gives you a trickle rather than nothing.

Ask next door. If their water is off too, it's the main and not your house — and there's nothing at your end to fix.

And in a freeze, no water at one cold tap while the others work usually means a frozen pipe rather than a supply problem. That's a different job and a different urgency.

If the street is off, it'll be on United Utilities' website before anyone picks up a phone: https://www.unitedutilities.com/

Anyone had a stopcock that turned out to be seized?

Published by CMG Heating & Plumbing, Bolton · Gas Safe 917962

posts.title: BWD — bwd_autumn_walkround
posts.caption:
Ten minutes outside this weekend, before the weather turns properly.

Gutters. Blocked ones spill straight down the wall every time it rains, and that wall doesn't get a chance to dry out all winter. Most damp patches on an outside wall start here.

The gully by the back door. Leaves sat in it means water backing up across the yard in heavy rain, and eventually finding a way somewhere it shouldn't.

Airbricks. Clear of soil, leaves, shrubs and anything stacked against the wall. They feed air to the underfloor space and, in a lot of houses, to a gas appliance.

Any overflow pipe. If one's dripping, something inside is filling past its stop point — and in a hard freeze that pipe can ice up and back the water into the loft instead.

None of it costs anything. All of it is a great deal cheaper than the thing it prevents.

What's the state of your gutters?

Published by CMG Heating & Plumbing, Bolton · Gas Safe 917962

posts.title: BWD - bwd_three_numbers
posts.caption:
Three numbers worth putting in your phone tonight. All free, and none of them much use once you actually need one.

0800 111 999 — the National Gas Emergency line. If you smell gas, that's the one. Answered 24 hours, and you are not charged for them coming out. People hesitate over that last bit and they shouldn't.

105 — power cut. Free from any phone, anywhere in England, Scotland and Wales, and it works out which network operator covers you so you don't have to. Nothing to do with who you pay your bills to.

United Utilities for water. Though check their website first — a burst main in the street is usually already on there before anyone picks up a phone.

Takes two minutes to add all three. Nobody looks up a number calmly in the dark with water coming through a ceiling.

Which one have you already got in your phone?

Published by CMG Heating & Plumbing, Bolton · Gas Safe 917962

posts.title: BWD — bwd_psr
posts.caption:
There's a free register a lot of people qualify for and never hear about.

It's called the Priority Services Register. Free, UK-wide, run by the energy and water companies, and it isn't means tested.

It's for anyone older, disabled, with a long-term illness, with young children in the house, or relying on electricity for medical equipment. Also, temporarily, for people going through something — bereavement, coming out of hospital, that sort of thing.

What you actually get: priority reconnection if the supply goes off, advance warning of planned work, a password so you know a caller at the door is genuine, bills in large print or braille if that helps, and in some cases alternative heating or hot meals during a long interruption.

The catch is that it's not one list. You sign up separately with your energy supplier, your electricity network operator and your water company.

You can also register on somebody else's behalf, which is the bit worth knowing if you've got an elderly parent.

Anyone on it already? Was it worth doing?

Published by CMG Heating & Plumbing, Bolton · Gas Safe 917962

posts.title: BWD — bwd_condensation_fixes
posts.caption:
Four things that genuinely cut condensation, and not one of them costs anything.

Lids on pans while you cook, extractor on, and left running a while after you've finished. A pan boiling without a lid puts a surprising amount of water into the air.

Bathroom door shut during a shower, fan left running afterwards. Shut door means the moisture goes out through the fan rather than wandering round the landing and settling on the coldest wall it can find.

Drying washing indoors is the big one. A wet load is litres of water, and it all ends up in the air. If it has to come indoors, one room, door shut, window cracked open.

And leave a gap behind furniture on outside walls so air can move over the cold surface. A wardrobe flat against an external wall is where the mould appears.

The principle is the same throughout: you're trying to get moisture out of the house, not wipe it off the window.

Which of those is the hardest one in your house? Drying washing, usually.

Published by CMG Heating & Plumbing, Bolton · Gas Safe 917962

posts.title: BWD — bwd_bleed_radiator
posts.caption:
Cold at the top, warm at the bottom means air in the radiator. Here's how to get it out properly.

Heating off first, and let it cool. Bleeding a hot system sprays hot water at you.

Key on the square at the top corner, cloth or a small pot underneath, quarter turn anticlockwise. Not a full turn.

Let it hiss. The second it starts running water rather than air, shut it.

Order matters more than people realise. Start with the radiator nearest the boiler and work outwards, downstairs before upstairs.

Then check the boiler pressure hasn't dropped below where it normally sits, because you've just let something out of a sealed system.

One thing worth saying plainly: bleeding is normal, but bleeding the SAME radiator twice a year isn't maintenance. A sealed system shouldn't be making air. If air keeps coming back, something is drawing it in and that's worth finding.

Got one you bleed over and over?

Published by CMG Heating & Plumbing, Bolton · Gas Safe 917962

posts.title: BWD — bwd_drinking_tap
posts.caption:
In a lot of older Bolton houses, only one tap is actually drinking water.

The kitchen cold tap normally comes straight off the rising main — the mains water coming into the house. That's the one.

In an older system the other cold taps, including the bathroom, may be fed from a tank in the loft. That tank is often open, usually dusty, and occasionally has things in it that you'd rather not think about while filling a glass.

Newer houses, and anything on a combi, are usually all mains-fed and it doesn't apply. But "usually" isn't "definitely", and if you don't know which yours is, then you don't know.

Either way, let it run for a moment until it's properly cold. Water sat in a pipe overnight has been sat in a pipe overnight.

Worth knowing if anyone in your house fills a kettle or a glass upstairs.

Do you know which system you've got?

Published by CMG Heating & Plumbing, Bolton · Gas Safe 917962

posts.title: BWD — bwd_water_meter
posts.caption:
Would a water meter save you money? There's a rough rule and then there's a proper answer.

The rule of thumb: if there are fewer people living in the house than there are bedrooms, a meter usually works out cheaper.

That's because an unmetered bill is based on the old rateable value of the property, not on what you actually use. So a couple in a three-bedroom terrace are often paying for a household that isn't there.

Flip it round and it works the other way. A big family in a small house is usually better off staying unmetered, because they'd be paying for every bath.

United Utilities has a calculator that gives you a proper comparison, and you can normally ask to switch and then change back within a set period if it doesn't suit. Worth checking the current terms rather than taking my word for that bit: https://www.unitedutilities.com/

Ten minutes either way, and for some households it's a meaningful amount.

Anyone switched and regretted it?

Published by CMG Heating & Plumbing, Bolton · Gas Safe 917962
